speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PERSONNEL OP DELEGATION TO CONFERENCE OF PRIME MINISTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members will know that I am proposing to leave tomorrow for London to attend the meeting of commonwealth prime ministers. As I have said previously in the house, this meeting will give an opportunity for an exchange of views on some very important questions, and it underlines the value of the commonwealth association as a medium for such exchanges. In turn these exchanges will make possible, I hope, more effective policies and actions for the attainment in our respective countries of the objectives of peace and greater human welfare which are basic for all the peoples of the commonwealth.
At this particular meeting questions of foreign affairs, and more particularly those concerned with Far Eastern matters, will occupy a great deal of attention. Recent developments in the Far East have underlined the seriousness of these issues. Because of that, and after certain messages to and from London, I have decided to ask my colleague the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) to accompany me to this conference. Of course it will be possible for him to return to Ottawa before the end of the conference if the situation here should appear to make that desirable.
As is customary I will also be attended at these meetings by the high commissioner for Canada in London. The under-secretary of state for external affairs, Mr. Leger, will be one of our advisers. I had hoped to include Mr. R. B. Bryce, the secretary to the cabinet, in that capacity, but because of his regrettable illness his place will be taken by Mr. Ross Martin, assistant secretary to the cabinet.
On economic matters we will be in close touch with our top economic advisers who are now attending the GATT meetings in Geneva, and it will not be difficult to have at least one of them join us in London when we reach the stage in the London meetings where we are dealing with that aspect of the agenda.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. Earl Rowe (Acting Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PERSONNEL OP DELEGATION TO CONFERENCE OF PRIME MINISTERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in view of the statement made by the Prime Minister I should like to ask him if he expects to discuss trade matters at this conference. Perhaps he might include the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) in his party.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PERSONNEL OP DELEGATION TO CONFERENCE OF PRIME MINISTERS
speechtext:
I should like to include all my colleagues in the house, but it so happens that that is not possible. In view of recent developments I would expect that much of our time will be taken up with a discussion of the international situation which we all look upon as being quite grave at this time. All of us appreciate the opportunity of taking counsel together as to what might best serve the interests of peace in the world.
The conference was not intended originally to operate as a continuation of the economic conference of two or three years ago, but I expect that that aspect of the world situation will also be under review. After the agenda has been settled at the first meeting we will know what time will be available for the consideration of that aspect of our affairs.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PERSONNEL OP DELEGATION TO CONFERENCE OF PRIME MINISTERS
speechtext: Is no one from the Department of Trade and Commerce going?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PERSONNEL OP DELEGATION TO CONFERENCE OF PRIME MINISTERS
speechtext: Top advisers of the departments of trade and commerce and finance, Mr. Mitchell Sharp and Mr. Plumptre, are already overseas.

subtopic: PERSONNEL OP DELEGATION TO CONFERENCE OF PRIME MINISTERS
speechtext: Are you taking a member of the opposition also?

subtopic: PERSONNEL OP DELEGATION TO CONFERENCE OF PRIME MINISTERS
speechtext: Are you available?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PERSONNEL OP DELEGATION TO CONFERENCE OF PRIME MINISTERS
speechtext: I am sure that might be quite helpful, but it has not yet become one of the traditions of these conferences between governments.

question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Mr. Speaker, the answer

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne offers private members an opportunity to direct the attention of the government, if that is possible, to serious grievances within our respective constituencies, and to express our views on outstanding problems in the life of this nation. This debate follows in the wake of the debate on external affairs which, in its high tone, its tense and dramatic moments, was certainly in keeping with the seriousness of the controversial problem being dealt with at that time.
The present debate is equally important because it comes closer to home and touches on problems that face our people every day of the week. I think we should remember that modern history records many nations have collapsed not so much from outside forces as from growing inequities, both social and economic, within the country, and failure to resolve those problems.
As a relatively new member of the house I have learned that a member's responsibilities to his constituents are varied. In this chamber, where we come together to reason and to give calm and considered study to the proper way in which to resolve our problems, it seems to me that the first responsibility of a member is to indicate objectively and honestly his views on the shortcomings of the government. Our nation's business, involving as it does the expenditure of some $5 billion of the taxpayers' money, involving decisions in domestic affairs affecting each and every one of us, involving decisions in external affairs as was indicated the other day during the external affairs debate, on matters which actually mould the destiny of our country-[DOT] such a nation's business calls for more than obedient approval of each and every measure presented by the government.
It seems to me there is little value in repeating pleasantries and being overcomplimentary in regard to past accomplishments. We certainly admit that the government has made some excellent moves in the past and that there are good men on the government side of the house. But no man is without fault and sometimes even good men following wrong policies lead us nowhere. I think democracy is sometimes cumbersome, but it does get things done; and if we are to achieve progress it can only be by continual prodding and constructive criticism in order that we may reach that perfection which is, after all, the objective and ultimate destiny of civilized man.

We are living in grave times and there are serious problems facing the country, such as the long, enduring and heavy burden of direct and indirect taxes and the general business recession, as evidenced by the business failures in our country during the first six months of 1954, which were 56 per cent higher than during 1953. The farmers' problems result from unsaleable crop surpluses that have accumulated. The drop in trade has been a sad development, resulting in an adverse balance of trade for the first six months of 1954 almost equal to the entire adverse trade balance for 1953. The colossal amount of credit buying that has taken place in our land recently indicates that our people are mortgaging their future earnings in order to acquire things which they need today. The growing high cost of government, the obvious trend toward centralization, and above all the lack of evidence that our present policies are capable of solving some of these problems, are matters for serious consideration. I believe that in the light of all this evidence there is no reason for any of us to consider all our activities here as being sacrosanct. Certainly we are proud of our accomplishments, and we have many of them in Canada. Surely, however, the credit goes to all of the people and not to one particular party. I believe that the progress that is being made in Canada is due, in the first place, to the courage of the early pioneers and the farsighted aspirations of people in an abundant land. Our progress has been made despite the small inducements offered in some of the government policies.
I wish to be fair in expressing my views. There are serious problems facing my constituents, and they are fresh in my memory. As I travelled around my constituency conversing with people I was led to believe that they look for a proper solution to some of their problems through the action of this house. With one or two exceptions the problems of my people are an integral part of the problems facing all the people in Canada.
I refer to the situation wherein there are hundreds of thousands of men and women in our country willing and able to work but unable to find employment. I refer as well to the hardship and distress that is the result of such a situation. We certainly were glad to see the speedy introduction by the government of measures to help alleviate the unemployment situation by the extension of unemployment insurance benefits. I believe we all agree that an increase in unemployment insurance benefits is not the solution to the unemployment problem. A proper solution would be the maintenance of conditions under which all hands and all 50433-37

Is it not thought-provoking that in a country such as this, with over four million square miles inhabited by only 15 million people, there should be unemployment? One would normally think our real problem would be to secure enough workers to handle the many tasks that have to be undertaken. I was disappointed as I stood, with others from this house, before the bar of the Senate and listened to the speech from the throne. Instead of a call to action, we heard a subdued review of past actions. In that speech, unemployment was referred to as some strange regional phenomenon. We all know it is more than that, Mr. Speaker. If unemployment has become a measuring rod of the seasons in Canada, then all I can say is that our seasons are becoming longer and longer and more depressing all the time. Blaming mother nature for our mistakes is, to my mind at least, a surprising new theory.
Then, of course, there are those who blame the newly arrived immigrants in our country as the ones who are responsible for unemployment. I believe there is little connection. These critics fail to realize that although some 174,000 people were admitted to Canada during 1954, many of them were dependent on those already in this country and did not replace anyone in a job. In addition, many of them have already returned to the countries from which they originally came. It is interesting to note also that some 50,000 Canadians emigrate each year to the United States, many of whom possess technical skills acquired through higher learning. With the unemployment situation as serious as it is I believe that exodus will become even more marked. We are thus losing human material which I believe is inexcusable.
What then are the real facts? I believe that unemployment is the result of various factors, not the least of which is our faltering economy resulting from the lack of sufficient purchasing power in the hands of our people to enable them to acquire the goods which they have produced and need. Much of this purchasing power is being arbitrarily removed from their hands by heavy taxation in order to sustain what I believe is the high cost of an ever-growing government.
I do not believe the Canadian boom was ever traceable to our policies alone, but was

The Address-Mr. Holowach the result of other factors. In an article appearing in The Challenge, a magazine issued by the Institute of Economic Affairs, New York University, volume III, No. 3, there is an interesting analysis by Frank A. Tinker, writing from Toronto where he served as United States vice consul. It reads as follows:
The Canadian boom was the result of a variety of factors: the backlog in consumer demand created by the war; the savage depletion of natural resources in other countries; the accompanying discoveries of, and investment in, these industrial materials in Canada; the creation of an industrial machine to meet the extraordinary demands; and the resultant population shifts.
. . . Much of the prosperity of Canada's citizens, which has not been as outstanding as the over-all picture suggests, is due to these artificial stimuli.
Today the factors which spurred the Canadian build-up no longer operate. Wartime scarcities have been eliminated. Industrial production in devastated countries has risen; recovery from war has filled the domestic gaps and has invaded those fields which previously were open only to the more fortunate, unscarred economies-like Canada's. The Korean and other Asian wars have been settled.
A little farther down this interesting comment appeared:
A large part of the difficulty lies in the tax program. The sound fiscal government of which Canadians have heard so much has been bought at the cost of assessments which a United States resident would consider outrageous and under which industry would suffer. The solvency of the government may be little solace to the Canadian who finds himself unemployed today partly because of it. This is not to say that a solvent government is bad. But a high-cost government which insists upon being supported through high taxes can be discouraging to say the least.
Perhaps some of us will not agree with all the statements made in that article. But I am sure we will agree that it is a disastrous human experience for us to realize that in time of war and blood-spilling we have prosperity, while in time of peace we always have a faltering economy.
What, then, are some of the answers? I am not one who knows all of them or even a large portion of them, but I think I know where to start. We start now by realizing that science and the inventive genius of man have been able to create an ever-increasing abundance of goods and services of every kind and variety. We have been able to solve the problem of production. Now the problem is to try to bring these goods within the reach of those people who need them.
I believe the real problem is for us to devise economic policies whereby these goods may be brought within the reach of those people whose incomes are being reduced because of the replacement of manpower by machines. It seems odd, Mr. Speaker, that on the one hand we all agree the progress of science is a good thing, we pass legislation in this house advocating shorter hours and

better working conditions, and we do this to eliminate the toil and hardship of the labouring group. Yet on the other hand in our fiscal policies we consider employment the only means of securing income to acquire the things people need. We are able to produce more, with fewer hardships and worries, but the paradox is that while on the one hand we are fostering scientific advancement which, after all, is aimed at the elimination of employment, on the other hand, we sustain an economic policy founded on the principle that the only way people can have incomes is by being employed.
There is proof that in modern civilization there will be increasing and ever-growing unemployment. I think attention has been drawn to this py farsighted statesmen ana public leaders. Here is an interesting article which appeared in the New York Times of January 17 and, while we may not agree with Mr. Reuther's political philosophy, I believe there is much food for thought in what he says. It is headed "Reuther Decries Brake on Output" and states:
He predicted that this year's output would fall $50,000,000,000 short qf. what it could be if there were enough customers to buy all the things our factories had the capacity to make.
He reiterated the C.I.O.'s support for maximum technological progress, but he warned that this progress could become a source of great suffering and social unrest unless the country applied "the same jet propulsion" to its thinking about human problems that was being focused on "automation", atomic energy and other scientific advances.
As evidence of the speed with which automatic methods were taking hold, Mr. Reuther told the unionists that the new Ford automatic engine plant at Cleveland already had been rendered "obsolete" by designs for even more efficient facilities.
"They can make a Ford engine block in only 15 minutes without a human hand touching it," Mr. Reuther declared, "and I am told they have on the drawing boards a plant that can cut the time down to 10 minutes."
He said the imbalance between what we could produce and what we could buy was becoming so acute that the manufacturers might find it necessary to set up plants to turn out "plastic consumers" to use the products for which there was no market.
My point is that this entire question must be faced realistically, and ways and means must be devised to make goods and services available to the people who are unable to find employment. At some future date unemployment may be inevitable. I do not think this necessarily implies idleness. It might spell out a new era wherein humanity will have longer rest periods and more leisure time to be devoted to physical and cultural pursuits, education and study, so as to enjoy a fuller and richer life.
Frankly, under our present fiscal policy there appear to be few remedies, unless the monetary reforms advanced by the Social Credit movement are given full and earnest

consideration. There might be some temporary alleviation of the problem by undertaking public projects. That should not entail going on a spending spree for the building of every project required in our country. In western Canada it should imply further financial assistance by the federal government to the respective provincial governments in order to induce them to undertake larger road building programs. This would absorb some unemployment, and certainly serve the needs of the country now and in the future.
I believe roads benefit the entire nation. Federal assistance in the matter of interprovincial roads is especially needed. On previous occasions I have drawn the attention of the government to the advisability of undertaking with the provincial governments the building of a road from Winnipeg by way of Saskatoon, Edmonton, Jasper park and the Yellowhead route, to the west coast. The rewards, both in times of war and peace, could not be measured in dollars and cents.
Second, I think we should design our policies to encourage consumption and production. In order to meet these requirements I submit that an early reduction in our taxes merits consideration. I believe the removal of many of the hidden taxes on commodities would bring these articles down to a level where people would be able to acquire them, thereby inducing consumption and production.
Apart from other benefits, it would restore some of the basic rights of the people to spend their own money instead of having governments spend it for them. I certainly disagree with those who believe that only by high taxes can we have high revenues. The reverse is often true. High taxes do not necessarily imply high revenues. I do believe that by a sensible reduction in taxation the government might well receive, through greater volume, what it now depends upon receiving through a high level of taxation.
Of course there are those in the house who indicate that because of our commitments by way of social services and defence costs, a reduction in taxation at this time would be improper. The movement to which I have the privilege of belonging is founded upon and dedicated to the well-being of the people. We look upon social services as the first responsibility of government. We consider it is the duty of government to protect our citizens against certain avoidable hazards of life and old age.
In the matter of defence it is true that we have no alternative but to carry on with our defence spending, in order to be secure in an uncertain world. However, let us remember that during 1953-54 the cost of 50433-374
The Address-Mr. Holowach national defence was reduced by some $126 million. However, that amount was absorbed by other departments. My point is that even if defence costs are reduced and if other government expenditures are not reduced accordingly just where in the world are we going? During 1952-53 these expenditures were $4-6 billion, and in 1953-54-55 they were approximately $5 billion. There is no denying that this government is growing larger and larger all the time.
Surely sizeable reductions in taxation could be brought about if the government would institute stringent policies of frugality to slice away some of the fatty tissues of government which are a consequence of the war years. I understand that at the present time some 22 crown corporations are being sustained by the taxpayers of Canada. The duties performed by many of these monopolies could well be performed by private enterprise if some incentive were given. In many cases the services performed by these corporations overlap the services offered by private enterprise.
Never before in our history have liberty and freedom had such meaning. We should realize that sometimes liberty and freedom disappear gradually through centralization and an ever-growing government until we reach a point where there is no turning back.
The forecast in the speech from the throne of increased basic rates and an increased permissible income under the War Veterans Allowance Act is commendable. So are the amendments to the Blind Persons Act to lower the age of eligibility and to increase income ceilings, and the conclusion of necessary arrangements with the various provincial governments in the matter of the Disabled Persons Act. They certainly deserve support from all members of this house. As the records indicate, we in this group have consistently fought for these measures. We realize that they have come late, but better late than never. We know they will be of assistance to many.
I regret that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler) is not in his seat, because I want to tell him how pleased the people of Edmonton were to hear that his department had decided to relocate and build new airport facilities in Edmonton. We trust that these measures will be undertaken with dispatch, as existing conditions certainly justify this move.
I regret the absence from the chamber of the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote), because I want to draw to his attention once more the need of an improved, enlarged or new post office building in Beverly, Alberta. The present building is no more than a shack, which if dismantled would hardly bring more than

The Address-Mr. Holowach a few hundred dollars on the used lumber market. On previous occasions I have drawn the attention of the minister to the need of further improvements to the building, or the erection of a new building. In no sense are these people asking for something which is unfair; they are asking for something which is completely justified in view of the limited facilities now available.
I am rather disturbed when I read statements which imply that a member's political affiliation determines the decision as to needs such as this being looked after. A report of this kind appeared recently in one of the Alberta papers. I quote from the Medicine Hat News of Saturday, January 15, 1955, as follows:
New Post Office Opened at Taber
Mayor Harry Veiner of Medicine Hat was master of ceremonies for the event, with Senator W. J. Stambaugh of Edmonton, the chief speaker, and representing the Minister of Public Works, the Hon. Robert H. Winters.
The senator read a telegram of regret from Mr. Winters for his inability to attend due to parliamentary duties, and congratulating Taberites on their patience in awaiting completion of such fine accommodation for an essential service.
J. Harper Prowse, leader of the Liberal party of Alberta, and a native of Taber, also sent regrets for his inability to attend.
Senator Stambaugh said the new federal building was a direct tribute to the prodding and enterprise of the late Senator W. A. Buchanan of Lethbridge.
"Without his interest I doubt if the contract for such a fine structure would ever have been let," observed Senator Stambaugh. "There would have been a new post office some day, but not such a fine building as this one. And then after Senator Buchanan passed to his reward, you had Mayor Veiner of Medicine Hat to carry forward demands upon Ottawa. He was largely responsible for having the post office section rushed through last fall and opening in time for some of the Christmas rush. Harry Veiner is well thought of in Ottawa and has been responsible for winning the government's attention to tlie needs of Medicine Hat constituency."
It was never my pleasure to know the deceased gentleman who is mentioned in this article, but I do know the high esteem and reputation which he enjoyed. I know the people of Canada looked upon him as a man of outstanding integrity and possessing statesmanlike qualities. If the late senator fought for a post office in Taber it was simply because Taber merited a post office. I am sure that were he alive, he would not approve his name being brought into a message such as was delivered recently at the opening ceremonies at Taber. Surely the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters) and the Postmaster General look with disfavour on this type of political drum-beating at the opening ceremonies of a public building in Canada.

I do believe that this newspaper report justifies a statement denying the assertion that political affiliation or political pressure determines the decisions in connection with the erection of public buildings.
Who is this man Harry Veiner who allegedly commands such tremendous influence in Ottawa? Is he not the same Harry Veiner who on two occasions was the Liberal candidate in that constituency and who, not once but twice, was rejected by the people of Alberta? It is stated that he is well thought of in Ottawa, and no doubt that is the reason for his rejection by the people of Alberta. Since when has he more authority to speak of the needs in that constituency, or to act as master of ceremonies at the opening, than the lawfully elected Social Credit member of that riding who, incidentally, was not even invited to attend the affair?
With such obvious political partisanship is it any wonder the people of Canada sometimes clamour for the reform of the other place? I believe such irresponsible statements are unfair to many hon. members in that other place who are more interested in Canada than in the well-being of any particular political party. I would suggest that if the hon. member from the other place is so interested in these matters he should be directing his efforts toward the construction of post office buildings in other places as well, and in this connection I would particularly direct his attention to the construction of a post office in the town of Beverly, Alberta.
I enjoyed listening to the speech by the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) a few days ago. He mentioned the need for the exercise of moral principles in our national life, and I believe all of us will agree that unless the men in high office in our national life adhere to moral principles there can be little hope of real progress in the future, because it is moral principles and decisions based on them that are the only valid and true measure of human progress in this country.
As we stand at the beginning of another year in the second half of this century, a century which has seen bloodletting, violence, wars, depressions, recessions, booms and busts, and which on the other hand has witnessed scientific advances without parallel in human history, we should bear in mind that our individual responsibility as members of this house is not entirely to the political parties to which we belong but to the people of this country. It also involves an understanding that there is poverty in our midst and that we must conquer unemployment.

It involves in external affairs the realization that there are many economically poor nations and others who are subjected to enslavement yet cry out for liberty and freedom. To champion their cause is to champion the cause of practically the most powerful allies the free world can muster, and to be indifferent to their plight would be completely unworthy of our Canadian heritage.
Toward the ultimate objective of securing a sound and prosperous Canada, and making Canada's contribution to a world condition in which there shall be peace, security, and the blessings of political freedom for all, the Social Credit movement is dedicated. We do not consider ourselves as having in any way a monopoly of virtue; we look upon all hon. members of the house, irrespective of their political faith, as having a role to play in meeting this challenge and in the achievement of peace throughout the world.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like first of all to extend my congratulations to the mover (Mr. Leduc) and seconder (Mr. Carrick) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Both hon. members are certainly worthy of the compliments which they have received from their colleagues in all parts of the house since this debate opened. In the discharge of their assignment they have both won an invaluable reputation for themselves and have proved to be a credit not only to their constituencies but to their respective cities of Montreal and Toronto, and to this parliament as well.
The subject matter which I wish to draw to the attention of hon. members at this time is one which has not been dealt with very often in this house in the past. It is also one which, in my estimation, deserves to be widely known to the Canadian public generally if it is to win the support of well informed Canadian public opinion.
It will be recalled that the eighth general conference of the United Nations educational, scientific and cultural organization, in other words UNESCO, was held at Montevideo, Uruguay, from November 11 to December 10, 1954. This was the first time a UNESCO general conference had met in South America. The choice of Montevideo was a fortunate one because it is the capital city of Uruguay, a country which rightly enjoys a reputation for its high standard of freedom and democracy.
The Canadian delegation which attended the conference was deeply impressed by the charm of that country and its people, and by the friendly warmth with which the Canadian representatives and the delegates of the other 71 member states were received.
The Address-Mr. Arsenault
Our delegation consisted of Mr. Sydney D. Pierce, Canadian ambassador to Brazil, who was chairman; the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo, Newfoundland (Mr. Carter); Dr. Philippe Panneton, of Montreal, widely known author and writer of many outstanding books on art, history and culture; Dr. Garnet T. Page, of Ottawa, a scientist and general manager of the Chemical Institute of Canada; Mr. F. K. Stewart, from Toronto, executive secretary of the Canadian Education Association; Dr. A. Vibert Douglas, a very distinguished iady and dean of women at Queen's University; Mr. Fulgence Charpentier, the Canadian charge d'affaires at Montevideo; Mr. Malcolm N. Bow, adviser from the Department of External Affairs; Mr. C. F. W. Hooper, from our Canadian embassy in Buenos Aires, who acted as general secretary of the delegation; and myself.
As I was designated vice-chairman of the Canadian delegation I had the privilege of serving as acting chief of the delegation during part of the conference. This was due to the fact that the economic conference of the organization of American states was held in Rio de Janeiro at about the same time as the UNESCO conference at Montevideo and the chairman of our delegation, Mr. Pierce, attended the Rio de Janeiro conference as an observer. May I express my gratitude to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and to the other members of the government for this assignment which I found to be an extremely valuable experience.
The Canadian delegation to Montevideo was a hard-working one. It was one which took an active part in all phases of the important tasks carried out by the general conference. Seldom in the past have I had the privilege of co-operating with a group of people so conscious of their responsibility toward Canada and so eager to discharge, to the best of their knowledge, competence and ability, the important and sometimes extremely tiresome duties which were assigned to each of them.
Members of our Canadian delegation participated with delegates from other member states on most of the committees or commissions set up by the plenary session of the general conference. Besides the plenary session, where Canada had five seats, members of our delegation sat on the program and budget commission, on the administrative commission and on the advisory committee, which are the four main working bodies of the general conference. The advisory committee to which I have just referred is a committee which is advisory on any question on which the program and budget

The Address-Mr. Arsenault commission wishes to receive technical advice. This advisory committee met two weeks before the official opening of the general conference and was attended by one of our delegates.
Canadian delegates have also been elected to the contribution committee and to the legal committee. This legal committee examines the constitutional and legal aspects of any resolution which involves constitutional or legal issues. A member of our delegation was also elected to the headquarters com,-mittee, which supervises matters pertaining to the new UNESCO headquarters which are to be erected at Paris, France. During the conference one of our delegates, Dr. Philippe Panneton, from Montreal, had the honour of being elected chairman of a working party.
The performance of the Canadian delegation at the recent UNESCO conference was, in my opinion, second only to that of the major powers. Yet in some instances when highly controversial issues were under consideration the Canadian attitude, and even our intervention as mediator upon the request of other nations, bestowed upon our delegation responsibilities which could not be more adequately discharged by any of the major powers, so great is the prestige that Canada enjoys today at the international level.
Having had the opportunity and the privilege of witnessing at close range the high consideration, the true confidence and the sincere esteem that other nations of the world have for Canada, for our Prime Minister and for our democratic government, I have returned from this UNESCO conference much prouder of our Canadian institutions and our sound administration, and much prouder to be a Canadian.
Before outlining some of the important decisions reached by the last conference of UNESCO at Montevideo, may I refer briefly to the historical background of UNESCO for the benefit of the readers of Hansard and that of the Canadian public generally. UNESCO, which is the abbreviation for the United Nations educational, scientific and cultural organization, was founded in London, England, in 1945 and the first general conference was held in Paris in November, 1946. Canada had joined UNESCO a few months prior to that time, on September 6, 1946.
In its early years UNESCO's energies were directed toward post-war rehabilitation, but in 1948 the organization turned toward the task of eradicating ignorance and illiteracy in the world. Dr. Jaime Torres-Bodet of Mexico, an international authority on mass education, was then appointed director general. He advocated an expanding program and budget

for a sustained attack on urgent international problems; but he resigned in 1952 when the general conference did not then approve the increased program and budget which he presented. Dr. Torres-Bodet, as we know, is now Mexican ambassador in Paris.
In July, 1953, Dr. Luther H. Evans of the United States was elected director general of UNESCO. One of his first endeavours was a reorientation of the organization's program. UNESCO now has an executive board of 22 members appointed by the plenary session. All candidates to the executive board must now first have the approval and the support of their respective governments. At this last UNESCO conference it was decided that 1955 and 1956 should be transitional years, and that the remodelled program should come into effect in 1957.

speechtext: If I have not made myself sufficiently clear I am sorry. By reorientation of UNESCO's program or the reorientation of UNESCO's activities and by the remodelled program which will come into effect in 1957, the director general of UNESCO and the secretariat as well have in mind a program which will concentrate on major projects of international importance, large projects, rather than on small projects of local interest.

speechtext: Could the hon. member give us a few examples of some of those projects?

speechtext:
Yes, I shall be glad to do so, Mr. Speaker. As examples of major projects of international importance I think I could probably mention measures devised to eradicate, for instance, racial discrimination, measures to sponsor better international understanding; or scientific research, for instance, to improve the standard of living. As an example of a small project of local interest I might perhaps mention assistance in the erection of a library or an archive somewhere in Asia or in the Middle East.
UNESCO, as we are all aware, is a specialized agency of the United Nations which has the task of bringing about a truly international appreciation of the various educational, scientific and cultural contributions of each country, and of the ways in which the people of the more fortunate lands may share

their techniques with and assist those in less developed areas. UNESCO's basic objective is to build the defence of peace in the minds of men through education, natural sciences, social sciences, cultural activities, mass communication, exchange of persons, and scientific assistance, which are made available to its member states and especially to the underdeveloped areas of the world. As is stated in the preamble to its constitution, "wars first originate in the minds of men". It is in the minds of men that the defences for peace must be erected. Therefore above all UNESCO is much concerned with what originates in the minds of men.
The entry to UNESCO in 1954 of the U.S.S.R., the Ukraine and Byelorussia, and the return of Poland, Hungary and Czechoslovakia to active participation brought the total membership of UNESCO to 72 nations. Some 1,200 delegates and technical advisers from all parts of the world attended the last UNESCO conference held in Montevideo. On the first day of the conference the Soviet delegation unsuccessfully urged the admission to UNESCO of Rumania and Bulgaria, and the rejection of the credentials of the representatives of nationalist China. However, the comparatively restrained and moderate statement of the Soviet spokesman was indicative of the attitude taken by the U.S.S.R. throughout the conference.
I must not forget to mention that the United States delegation also avoided provocation and concentrated on supporting increased technical aid to underdeveloped countries. Three resolutions on atomic energy offered another opportunity for political argument on such questions as banning atomic weapons, disarmament, the harmful effects of radiation, the control of nuclear energy and so forth. However, thanks to the co-operative spirit of all concerned it was possible to combine the three resolutions into one which authorized the director general of UNESCO to extend full co-operation to the United Nations on questions concerning the peaceful use of atomic energy. The joint resolution was, therefore, approved unanimously.
A Soviet resolution on measures to prevent the use of mass communication for the propaganda of war seemed certain to create real trouble until the Soviet delegation finally joined Canada, Colombia, Czechoslovakia, France, India, Lebanon, Mexico, the United Kingdom and the United States in sponsoring an alternative resolution on freedom of information. The resolution was approved unanimously, but the various interpretations of the operative paragraph, which invited the member states "to take the necessary measures to ensure freedom of expression
The Address-Mr. Arsenault and to remove barriers to the free flow of undistorted information" somewhat circumscribed the enthusiasm with which this Soviet concession had been greeted.
Throughout the conference there was an insistent demand from underdeveloped countries for a substantial extension of UNESCO's program and a large increase in the budget. The contributions of new members provided additional revenue and made possible expansion of the program and budget without an increase in the individual contributions of member states. By an overwhelming majority vote the conference approved an assessment level of $20 million for 1955 and 1956, an increase of approximately $2 million over 1953 and 1954. The redistribution of contribution percentages, as new members joined UNESCO, caused Canada's percentage to decline from 3-54 per cent to 2-77 per cent. The amount of the Canadian contribution for 1955 and 1956 will be approximately $554,000, compared with more than $600,000 in 1953 and 1954.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit another question? What is the basis of the contributions of the various members of UNESCO?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The contributions of member states of UNESCO are established on the same basis as the contributions of member states of the United Nations. The population and national income of each country are taken into account. There are other factors which are considered, such as loss sustained during the last war and so forth. As I have just mentioned, our percentage of contribution was reduced this year to 2-77 per cent, while our percentage of contribution to the United Nations is 3-60 per cent, if I recall correctly.

speechtext: What was the reason for the decrease in our contribution?

speechtext:
The reason for the decrease in the percentage was the new members that joined UNESCO. I think I can answer the question of the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer) by saying that there are 60 nations of the world which are members of the United Nations, while there are 72 countries which belong to UNESCO. The entry of the U.S.S.R., Byelorussia and the Ukraine, bringing with it their contributions, caused Canada's percentage to decrease from 3-54 per cent to 2-77 per cent. Of course our contribution to the United Nations is higher than that to UNESCO because the budget of the United Nations is in round figures $40 million, with our contribution being about $1,500,000, while the total budget

The Address-Mr. Arsenault of UNESCO is in round figures $10 million and our contribution is approximately $300,000 a year.
Some of the projects which have been approved by the conference and that are of greatest interest in Canada have to do with matters pertaining to education. There is the continuation of the international fundamental education centres at Patzcuaro, Mexico, and Sirs el Laiyana, Egypt. A regional conference on compulsory education will be held in Latin America during 1956. Teaching about both the United Nations and human rights will be stressed. Assistance to member states in the development of adult education, toward better international understanding, was authorized, and special consideration will be given to selected summer schools in underdeveloped areas, and those for women students.
In the development of youth education for social responsibility and international understanding, a system of associated youth enterprises will be instituted during 1955 and 1956. Subventions to 11 international educational organizations were approved.

speechtext: I wonder whether the hon. member would permit a question at this point. I was interested in his reference to centres of international education where fundamental education was taught. He mentioned these schools as being in Mexico and Egypt. Could he tell us something of what is taught at these schools?

speechtext:
I shall be glad to. The international fundamental education centres at Patzcuaro, Mexico and Sirs el Laiyana, Egypt, deal with the general form of education, education in the broad sense of the term. The centre at Patzcuaro, Mexico, alone takes care of the whole of Latin America, while the one at Sirs el Laiyana, Egypt, serves not only the Egyptian area but the whole of the Middle East. The population of those areas of the world are taught at those two centres, for example, how to maintain health; how to use their natural resources to best advantage in order to raise their standard of living; how to develop their agricultural resources, etc. In a broad sense that is what we mean by fundamental education.
Under the heading of natural science, the conference agreed that arid zone research should be accelerated. A substantial increase was voted in the budget for this activity. Surveys of the arid zones in Latin America, the Middle East and south Asia will be examined by committees of experts in an effort to co-ordinate research on this subject.

The proposed campaign against cancer was one of the most controversial items in the entire UNESCO program. It was first approved, then rejected, and finally accepted under the new title of "basic research on cellular growth."
The conference expressed keen interest in the work of the international council of scientific unions. A study conference on science teaching will be held in south Asia in 1955.
Subventions to the council of international organizations of medical sciences, to the union of international engineering associations, to the general assembly of the international union of biochemistry and to the international geophysical year were approved.
Under the heading of social sciences, it was decided that the development of social science teaching will be encouraged, with particular attention being given to direct aid to member states and the teaching of economics at universities.
The conference decided to intensify its work in the field of human rights and minorities, and to initiate a world-wide campaign to eradicate racial discrimination. Subventions were granted also to eight international social science organizations or institutions.
Under the heading of cultural activity, the conference authorized an analysis of the use of radio and television in cultural programs and a study of traditional cultures in southeast Asian communities which are undergoing rapid technological changes.
It authorized also an inquiry into the teaching of the humanities. Comparative studies of methods used in education through arts and crafts in industrial and rural areas will be conducted in Sweden, Germany and the U.S.S.R.
Underdeveloped countries that have requested assistance will be aided in establishing libraries and archives, the education of librarians and the microfilming of library or archival materials. During 1955 a seminar on public library development will be held in India, and a regional conference on the exchange of publications will be held in Latin America. The aid to member states such as Burma, India and Pakistan, for example in the development of museums, was approved and assistance was authorized to the international council of museums for the international exchange of exhibitions.
The conference recommended maintenance of the necessary services for the implementation of the universal copyright convention as well as for the protection of cultural property

in the event of armed conflicts. Subventions to 11 international cultural organizations were approved.
Under the heading of mass communication, such as the press, radio, television, the continuation of all UNESCO's activities for the promotion of international understanding was authorized. Continued efforts to procure support for proposed international agreements on the free flow of information were urged, and the preparation of a recommendation to member states on the free movement of persons was authorized. A substantial appropriation was provided for expert missions and fellowships. Under the heading of exchange of persons, priority will be given to the underdeveloped countries in the awarding of fellowships.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, under the heading of general resolutions; the conference considered the development of national commissions to be one of the most important questions on the agenda. A study of the structure and methods of work of existing commissions, the resources at their disposal, and the difficulties they were encountering was authorized. All member states were urged to improve the operation of their national commissions.
At this point may I recall, Mr. Speaker, that in chapter 25 of the report of the royal commission on the arts, letters and sciences which was tabled in this house in June, 1951, the commission summarized certain disabilities which, in its view, seriously handicapped arts and letters in Canada. One of the gaps in our national equipment in relation to the arts, letters and social sciences which the royal commission cited was the following, and I quote from pages 372 and 373 of the report:
Although Canada is a member of the United Nations educational, scientific and cultural organization, there is not yet established in Canada any form of national commission for UNESCO; an undertaking to create such a commission or an equivalent forms part of the UNESCO constitution, which Canada has accepted.
Canada has been a member of UNESCO since 1946, and has not yet established a national commission such as that prescribed by the UNESCO constitution and recommended by the royal commission. It will be recalled that the royal commission recommended the creation of a council for the arts, letters and sciences which, together with other varied and complex duties, would act as a national commission for UNESCO. Many of the duties of the proposed Canada Council would be concerned precisely with those matters of greatest concern to UNESCO, so that by the creation of a single body wasteful duplication would be avoided.
The Address-Mr. Arsenault
It seems obvious that the circumstances and considerations which led the royal commission to make this recommendation are still valid. As at September 1952, out of the 65 member states of UNESCO only three countries in addition to Canada had not established national commissions. They were Arabia, Korea, and Czechoslovakia. So long as we do not have some kind of national body, organized for the purpose to which I have just referred, we shall be failing in our undertaking to UNESCO, and we shall be taking only a very inadequate part in the UNESCO programs.

Through the national commission for UNESCO, which would represent Canada as a whole, as well as the various literary, artistic and scientific organizations in Canada, the Canadian people would become much better informed of the achievements and purposes of UNESCO and, it seems quite clear, would be better prepared to advance, both within this country and internationally, the objectives of the UNESCO constitution, which Canada is under obligation to foster.

Undoubtedly all important matters of policy would still be determined by the government, but on a very considerable number of matters the advice of the interested voluntary organizations in Canada would be of the greatest value. Mr. Speaker, this opportunity to take part in the debate on the speech from the throne gives to a member an occasion at the beginning of each session to survey the position of parliament, to survey the issues to come before parliament, and to reach some conclusions and form some opinions on the role which parliament generally is playing in the affairs of Canada. This opportunity is the more significant since Canada is assuming an important place in the affairs of the world. Therefore I think it appropriate that when taking part in this debate a member should make some remarks in relation to the position of parliament and the relationship between parliament and the government. Speaking for myself at any rate, I find considerable cause for deep concern in the present relationship between the government and parliament and in the attitude toward parliament shown by the present government over the years in which I have been here.
50433-38J
The Address-Mr. Fulton
Very often-and perhaps more so on this side than on the other-we members object to the way in which the government seeks to control parliament, and to the way in which it ignores parliament. At the beginning of this session when there is confronting us a revision of the rules of the house, a committee for which has been set up, I think we should express some conclusions and indicate some objections to the way in which this process has been going on.
I do not wish to open my remarks in too partisan a spirit, but nevertheless I feel I am justified in saying that by and large the manner in which the government ignores parliament and the way in which the government attempts to control parliament is unfortunately approved of by the majority on the government side. For instance, I refer to such incidents in the past as the statement made by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) that the government will give to parliament only such information as it sees fit to give unless the decision as to what should or should not be given to parliament is disagreed with by the majority. As I have stated, unfortunately the government controls that majority and the majority appears willing to accept that control. As a result the government is enabled to carry out its policy of refusing information to parliament, of refusing to take parliament into its confidence and of refusing to bring before the representatives of the people for discussion those matters upon which we are entitled to be asked to form a decision.
Indicative of this trend was the refusal to call parliament last fall when there were important issues affecting the country which were giving cause for great concern on the part of our people. I am not going to revive the debate which was concluded yesterday, but I cannot fail to refer to the fact that parliament and the people were kept in ignorance of the real facts with respect to the German treaty.
There are further grounds for the objections which I now make in that when the government does call parliament it treats it with what amounts to contempt. Their attitude is a reminder of the principle behind the statement made on one occasion in this house by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), who said, "If we want to get away with it who can stop us?". No minister in a government which had a proper appreciation of the position of parliament and of the relations of a government to parliament would have dreamed of using such words.

The Address-Mr. Fulton
This attitude of the government toward parliament is further demonstrated by the numerous interruptions which have taken place already in this debate. It is an accepted principle, which unfortunately is not followed by this government in practice, that the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne affords to members of parliament an opportunity to indicate whether or not they have confidence in the government. For that reason the normal business of the session is not proceeded with until that debate has been concluded.
I am not in any sense criticizing the laying before the house of the details of the government's program for the session while the throne speech debate is in progress. We are in complete and thorough agreement with that new practice. What I am referring to is the interruptions which have occurred in this debate for the purpose of taking up other matters. Several such interruptions have taken place at this session, and they have had the effect of reducing the significance of this debate, which in effect is an affront to parliament and an insult to its rights.
One can see in this interference with the throne speech debate the natural outcome of the government's attitude to parliament. The Prime Minister and the government said that there was nothing urgent enough to warrant the calling of parliament last fall. That argument was repeated yesterday. And yet already the throne speech debate has been interrupted because it was said that now we are here there are matters of such urgency that they require immediate attention and the government insisted upon laying aside this debate in order to have the other matters dealt with.
Only yesterday we heard the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) tell us that the consideration of the matter of the German treaty then under discussion was not really of sufficient urgency to warrant an earlier calling of parliament; yet he was speaking in the course of a debate which he had asked to have held at this time and which could only be held by interrupting the proper and normal business of parliament. In the same way this throne speech debate was interrupted earlier for the purpose of considering amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act.
There is not one of us who would deny the urgency of that matter in the light of the situation which the government has allowed to come about. But it is nothing short of absurd, it is nothing short of an affront to parliament, and is an indication of the government's attitude toward parliament to say, on the one hand, that there is nothing of such concern
IMr. Fulton.]
that parliament should be called early to consider it-to indicate in effect that parliament could not make much of a contribution to the matter in any event-and then to get us down here and say, "Now you are here, these matters are in fact of such urgency that we have to interrupt the proper and normal process by which parliament proceeds in order to take up these emergency matters".
In the same way in this session we have already seen a departure from another principle the preservation of which, I submit, is essential if parliament is to be in a position and have the authority whereby it is enabled to deal effectively with the government, which after all is or should be its responsibility. I refer to the principle of ministerial responsibility and cabinet solidarity. After all, if this parliament and the country are to be confronted with a series of statements by ministers, each of which is at variance with the other, it becomes impossible for parliament to decide the government's stand on a particular issue and thus to debate the merits or demerits of that stand.
We have seen increasing indication over the past few years of a serious departure from this principle of cabinet solidarity. I do not think it has been more conspicuously revealed than it was a couple of years ago in connection with the payment of $65 million to the wheat farmers of the prairies. At that time we had the Minister of Trade and Commerce saying one thing and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) saying diametrically the opposite in connection with the government's policy in that regard. When those two gentlemen found themselves in such an absurd position, they finally had to scramble out of their fix as best they might by saying, "Well, we have what we regard as a good Prime Minister; we will leave it to him and he will save the situation".
We have had an almost exact repetition of that absurd position this session. That was in the discussion of an important matter, the construction of the dam on the South Saskatchewan river. On the one hand, the Prime Minister has said the government does not feel it can conscientiously recommend to parliament that it is in the national interest to proceed with this matter; but on the other hand, we have the Minister of Agriculture out there carrying on negotiations with the government of Saskatchewan. What are the people to conclude the government believes? How are the people of Canada, or the parliament of Canada as representatives of the people, to arrive at any understanding of the nature of government policy in the light of confusion resulting from the fact that the government no longer speaks with a consistent voice?

We see another example of the government's overbearing attitude to parliament in the further refusal of information by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) with respect to the subjects which are to be discussed at the forthcoming conference of the commonwealth prime ministers. As has already been stated, apart from recent very pressing and immediate problems of international relations, there is no more important problem for this country than the question of intercommonwealth trade, and our trading relations within the commonwealth and the orientation of our trading channels generally.
Yet the Prime Minister refuses to afford parliament the opportunity of discussing the policies Canada should follow, refuses to give any indication of the position he intends to take on behalf of this government at that conference. Parliament is refused an opportunity to express its agreement or disagreement with those policies, to which however, we shall no doubt be committed. All that the Prime Minister tells us is that he, after all, is not going over there to make things any worse. The result of that attitude, Mr. Speaker, certainly means-if that is his attitude-that even if he tried he could make things no worse but he certainly is not going to make them any better. I suggest the Canadian parliament have a right to expect of their government and of their Prime Minister the expression of a more realistic concern with the problems which are exercising the Canadian people.
Then when the government, having treated parliament not only on this occasion but over past years with contempt, finally got around to calling parliament, they laid before us a throne speech which, by its conspicuous failure to deal with more pressing problems, is itself a further affront to a legislative body claiming any measure of independence and discretion.
In my view the most conspicuous failure of the throne speech is the failure even to mention one of the most outstanding and vexed problems of the day, the problem of dominion-provincial relations.
But perhaps on reflection, Mr. Speaker, it may be concluded that it is after all not surprising that there is no mention made of this subject, because in no respect has the record of the Liberal party and of the Liberal government been more shameful than in this field. There is no field in which that party has done more by playing politics to endanger national unity and bring relations between the various parts of our country almost to the breaking point.
It is a record in which unfortunately the Prime Minister, by his recent deliberate and
The Address-Mr. Fulton calculated reversal of policy and attitude, is now shown to have played a leading part, and in which he has had the enthusiastic backing of several members of his cabinet.
It has, of course, been for many years a deliberate part of Liberal policy to exploit the differing sentiments of differing parts of this country-always under the guise of fostering national unity. They have brought relations between the dominion and the provinces to the breaking point; they inflame the passion of one section of the country against another; they encourage resentment by the provinces against the dominion; they play off one part against the other and all the parts against the whole-then at the last moment, when the situation has reached a position of imminent disaster, they make a concession to avert a disaster which they themselves have created. Then they and their spokesmen, and the propaganda sheets which so assiduously foster the Liberal cause throughout the country, cynically seize upon the very concession they have made and boast that they have made another contribution to national unity thereby.
We have seen this process repeated once more and carried to the very ultimate just recently. We have seen a subject vital to the welfare of the nation-we have seen the welfare of the nation itself-used for political advantage by this Liberal government. In this whole process the Prime Minister has unfortunately played a leading part.
I refer, of course, to the method by which this government has dealt with relations between the dominion and the provinces, and particularly with the province of Quebec, over the taxation problem. There we see revealed in the most startling manner the way in which the Liberal government, under its Prime Minister, has been playing politics with a national issue for partisan political advantage.
To establish the truth of this assertion one has but to compare the statements and attitude of the Liberal leader last summer and fall with his actions in January of this year.
Last fall-and he must have known that six by-elections were in the offing in various parts of Canada in English-speaking or largely English-speaking ridings-the Prime Minister embarked on a course which constituted an appeal to English-speaking Canada, by attacking the premier of Quebec. So we had the sabre-rattling speech at the Reform club in the city of Quebec on September 16.
Then we were told there could never be one arrangement with one part of Canada and another arrangement with the others. Then the principle was enunciated that the whole was greater than any of the parts. Then we

The Address-Mr. Fulton were told that the Prime Minister had thrown down the gauntlet, challenged the premier of Quebec, and embarked on a battle to the death for the sacred principle of Canadian unity.
And how the ruse worked! For it was a song that has an appeal in many quarters- the battle song of the Liberal party which has led them to so many election victories: the song of national unity over-all while provoking national disharmony in all the parts. And nowhere, of course, does the sort of appeal made on September 16 have a greater attraction than in quarters where the feelings of the province of Quebec are not understood, and where the people have been exposed to years of the Liberal propaganda-the propaganda which states in one part of the country that Uncle Louis and his Liberal government are the saviours of the country from the wiles of the Conservatives, who are prepared to co-operate too closely with the premier of Quebec, while at the same time saying in Quebec that Uncle Louis-Papa Louis-is the saviour of his country from the wickedness of the Conservatives who will rob them of their heritage.
And so, to the advantage of the by-elections, and of the Liberal party, there was sung by the Prime Minister the battle song of anti-Duplessis; anti-tax concession; and the preservation inviolate and unchanged of the existing tax deals. And the ruse worked again.
Up until now, Canadians have taken the Prime Minister at his word and at the evaluation placed upon him by the Liberal party and its propagandists. I believe the Canadian people, even yet, are hardly able to realize the extent to which they were misled and misinformed in their appreciation of him and what he was doing.
Today, the by-elections being safely over, a completely different and diametrically opposite position has been taken by the Prime Minister. The very things we were led to believe he would never do are now being done.

I see that my hon. friends do not like this very much. I did not suppose that they would. But we should look at what was said before and compare it with what is now being done. You will find, Mr. Speaker, that the proposal now made does involve the payment of different rates of federal tax by people in receipt of the same income residing in different provinces. To appreciate the extent of the hypocrisy of the Liberal party in dealing with the question of national unity, one has only to consider the extent to which the passions and prejudices of the rest of the nation were influenced by their spokesmen before the by-elections, and compare their earlier statements with their present actions. In 1954 the actions and proposals of the Quebec premier were everywhere ridiculed and condemned. In 1955, after the by-elections, they are in large part accepted, though in a different form. It should be noted that the premier of Quebec never went so far as to suggest that federal taxpayers in Quebec should have a lower federal tax rate than those living elsewhere, which will now be the case.

Let us compare some of the statements made. In 1954 the then minister of finance said in this house on April 6:
The principle underlying the suggestion that provincial tax should generally be allowed as an offset against federal tax strikes at the very root ol the system of federal-provincial tax agreements which have been developed in this country.
But in 1955, on January 14, in a letter to the premier of Quebec the Prime Minister says:
. . . we intend to propose to parliament a reduction of the federal tax for all taxpayers of a province having a provincial tax, whether or not they have to pay the provincial tax.
In 1954, the Prime Minister, in the speech already referred to-a speech which could only appeal to those parts of Canada where the Quebec premier was not popular, and in a speech deliberately insulting to the premier of that province-based . his appeal on the principle that he and his government would never offer to the people of one province any concession or benefit not available to the people of another. But in 1955 the Prime Minister does exactly the opposite; for in 1955 he says this, and these words can be found at page 230 of Hansard:
We also Intend to propose that Income tax payers who have actually paid a provincial income tax on their 1954 income-
And this applies only to the taxpayers of Quebec.
-be allowed a deduction up to 10 per cent of their federal tax.
You will recall further, Mr. Speaker, that in 1954, before the by-elections and in this house the Prime Minister told us-and he was echoed in this by certain of his colleagues, one in particular-that no good purpose would be served by holding a further dominion-provincial conference. But in 1955, after the by-elections, he tells us that a conference will be a good thing and that he proposes to call one at the earliest possible date.
Mr. Speaker, seen now in this light, seen now in its true perspective, seen after it has served its purpose for the political advantage of the Liberal party, this Reform club speech and the whole attitude and conduct of the Prime Minister stand out as one of the sorriest examples of conduct the only result of which was to fan the flames of racial prejudice and to sow the seeds of national discord and disunity-although it may have resulted in a temporary political advantage.
Then what of that other exponent of Liberal political principles, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson). This great emancipator-you will remember, Mr. Speaker, how he was going to free us from the bonds of servile colonialism which he said still bind
The Address-Mr. Fulton us with respect to our constitution, and how he called a conference of the dominion and the provinces to find ways and means of amending the constitution; you will recall how he dropped that proposal like a hot brick back in 1950, when he found that once again the interests of his own party and those of the nation did not coincide, and how he once again subjugated the national interest to his party's political interests-in respect of this matter of the tax deal the great emancipator has found himself reduced to the position of a third-rate slave trader.

All that is nesessary is that he be a resident of British Columbia and of school age.

The government proposes to extend the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act for two years, 1955 and 1956. Payments will be made on a different basis than formerly. The formula for assistance payments to gold mines consists of two factors. The first is the rate of assistance, and the second the portion of the production to which the rate of assistance applies. The proposed new bill maintains these two parts, but they have been somewhat simplified.
The rate of assistance has been revised and will be the amount that is two-thirds of the amount by which the average cost of production of gold from the mine during the year exceeds $26.50 per ounce.
