I wonder if I could say a few words, Mr. Speaker, on the statement the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) has just made. First of all, I should like to say how glad I am that the great industrial struggle is over, as I am sure every member in this house is. During the time of this strike I have been thinking that huge industrial strikes of this kind, long drawn out, are perhaps in the same position as modern wars, that nobody wins.
Having had a settlement of this dispute after it has cost the parties concerned so much, possibly this would be a good time for some sort of committee-I do not know what you would call it, public relations or something of that kind-to continue explorations into the possibility of finding some way of dealing with these disputes after they have gone through the usual procedure and before a strike is called. I do not know whether or not I have made my idea clear to the minister, but I cannot think of anyone better than the

The Address-Mr. Maclnnis minister himself to approach the leaders of the trade unions and industry to discuss the possibility of avoiding long strikes of this kind in the future.
Shortly before my remarks were interrupted by the dinner recess I referred to the fact that newly arrived immigrants to Canada were provided with board and room if they were unemployed. I- hope I did not give the impression that I objected to that being done. Certainly I do not, and I hope it will continue to be done as long as it is necessary. We should not bring people to this country unless we are sure there will be work for them. If there is no work for them, we should look after them.
What I have been complaining about is that we seem to be doing more for the newly arrived immigrants than for the residents of Canada. During my remarks I mentioned conditions in Vancouver. I have here a pamphlet issued by the Canadian Welfare Council urging that something be done to provide a public assistance program for the employable unemployed. I want to draw to the attention of the minister and the house some of the conditions mentioned by the Canadian Welfare Council. As I said-and I mentioned the city of Vancouver-the first paragraph in this program says:
Appeals by the Salvation Army in North Bay "for donations of soup-bones, vegetables, and bread to feed transient men and their families", the re-introduction of used clothing drives in Windsor, the opening of soup-kitchens in Vancouver, and similar reports reaching the Canadian Welfare Council in recent weeks from many parts of the country, are evidence of the fact that there are still a great many unemployed workers in Canada whose essential needs are not being met.
I was wondering why the words "there are still a great many unemployed workers in Canada" are in here; but I imagine they are here because of the optimistic reports made from some government sources that the unemployment situation is on the up and up, although it is on the down and down.
Commenting further on the situation, this pamphlet goes on to say:
The head of a family who is denied help by municipal authorities on the ground that he is "employable" may be referred from one organization to another to beg for clothes, groceries for his family, or money to stave off eviction. He may stand in line for a bowl of soup to relieve the pressure on the food supply at home. Even though he can manage to keep his family alive, the loss of morale due to stop-gap measures, the need to seek help from several agencies, each meeting only part of his need, tend to discouragement and weakening of family ties.
I submit that these are the conditions which now prevail in this rich country, where so many of us are so well provided for and so happy. And it is, truly, a sad commentary on our social organization and our social

outlook that we should allow people to have to beg for soup bones and to have to beg for other people's cast-off clothing. Surely when they have to do those things it must leave scars on the human personality that will take many, many years of good living to eradicate.
The Canadian Welfare Council is suggesting that the various governments-municipal, provincial and federal-should organize a conference at which this situation could be discussed. And may I draw attention again to what I said quite recently in this chamber on another occasion, that how quickly and how effectively we act in this matter should not depend upon whether there are 20,000 unemployed or 200,000 unemployed. The needs of 20,000 are just as urgent, and it is just as necessary to look after their needs in a humane and civilized way as it is to look after the needs of 200,000 or 300,000, or whatever it may be.
Now I shall read a very short paragraph summing up the view of the Canadian Welfare Council. It says:
The Canadian Welfare Council urges all governments in Canada, federal, provincial and municipal, to take such action as may be required to bring about a conference on the subject of public assistance for the employable unemployed, in order to determine the most appropriate allocation of governmental responsibilities for meeting the needs of those unemployed persons not protected by the provisions of the Unemployment Insurance Act and to ensure that a program for this group is established with the least possible delay.
I give my support to that; but I submit that it is not enough at this time. We cannot wait now. As the editorial in the Vancouver Province says, empty stomachs cannot wait. We cannot wait now for a conference of this kind. We want something done now, done today, in order that we may eradicate this shame from our country.
The federal government in 1945 gave a firm commitment to the people of Canada that it would take the responsibility for dealing with this matter of employable unemployed. After learning the lessons of the depression, and after learning the lessons of abundance during five or six years of war, the government came out with an analysis of that situation, and a program to meet it.
I am going to put it on the record again and, although it has been done before, I make no apology for doing so now. Before the dinner recess I read a short paragraph from this book "Proposals of the Government of Canada, August 1945", where they pointed out that the war came before solutions to our main problems were reached. Let me read just a little more:
The difficulties of the depression were quickly submerged in the great national effort against aggression abroad.

The Address-Mr. Maclnnis
Now there is aggression at home, the aggression of unemployment. It continues:
The winning of the war became a single dominant purpose to which all lesser demands and objectives were subordinated. The obstacles to united effort were removed by the willingness and patriotic desire of all groups to accept sacrifices and restrictions in order to ensure victory.
Now, I do not expect people to act in peace just the same as they do in war, even if the need is to relieve the distress of their fellow man. But people who stand in the way should be exposed by the government of this country, in the same way as they would have been exposed if they had stood in the way during the time we were at war. That is the government's responsibility; and unless they are willing to do that, there will always be selfish people who will stand in the way of progress.
I continue to read:
The federal government was responsible for the organization of the national effort and there were no limitations upon its power to do so. These circumstances and the co-operative spirit of the provincial governments made it possible to overcome, or temporarily to set aside, the factors which have impeded the development of solutions to difficulties of the past.
Let me draw the attention of the house to this next sentence-and it is not ten years yet since this was said. It represents the government's opinion in 1945. The people of Canada were looking forward to this, and the day of disillusionment comes in 1955:
The accomplishment of our aims in the post-war period must, no less than in war, be an object of national endeavour.
I ask the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg), and any other minister sitting in front of me, if that is what they are doing today. Is that what they are doing?
The accomplishment of our aims in the post-war period must, no less than in war, be an object of national endeavour.
Well, I am sure, if it were, they would get a lot of help from the people of Canada. As I said before, there might be some selfish persons who would stand in the way; but the help and co-operation they would get from the rest of the people of Canada would be so great that those obstacles would be insignificant.
Then it continues:
Success in the attainment of high levels of employment, increased welfare and security, is dependent upon the fruitful co-operation between all governments and groups in the country. It is the responsibility of government to pursue policies that create conditions In which the initiative, energy and resourcefulness of individual citizens can achieve rising standards of life.
And if that is not accomplished, then it logically follows that it is the duty of this government itself to do those things which
private enterprise fails to do. That is its responsibility, either to do that or to abdicate.
Let me draw the attention of the house to the commitments which the government gave to the people of Canada in 1945, to be found on page 7 of the "Proposals of the Government of Canada" which I have mentioned already. These are:
To achieve the large objectives we must set for export trade, domestic consumption, private and public investment will require a closely integrated effort. The general principles guiding this effort must be explicit and clear as they will form the framework within which the specific plans and arrangements must be worked out. To this end the government briefly sets forth the basic principles underlying its proposals.
In familiar terms, our objectives are high and stable employment and Income, and a greater sense of public responsibility for individual economic security and welfare.
Who is taking responsibility today for the more than 300,000 unemployed?
Realization of these objectives for all Canadians, as Canadians-
Not just Canadians who are employed or in business, but all Canadians, which would mean Canadians who are unemployed.
-is a cause in which we would hope for national enthusiasm and unity.
I have pointed out to the minister and the government that they will have national enthusiasm and unity the moment they start to do something; but they will not have any enthusiasm or unity as long as they just sit and look at the problem and hope that something will happen to solve it for them. I continue to quote:
The government has clear and definite views on how these objectives can be attained.
I hope the ten years which have intervened since 1945 have not dimmed that clear and definite view.
These views may be summarized very briefly as, first, to facilitate private enterprise to produce and provide employment; secondly, to promote bold action by the state-
Just think of this government promoting bold action to provide for Canadians.
-in those fields in which the puolic interest calls for public enterprise in national development; thirdly, to provide, through public investment, productive employment for our human and physical resources when international and other conditions adversely affect employment;
I say that those conditions are here now; international and other conditions are adversely affecting employment and this is the time when the government should act as it committed itself to the people of this country in 1945 to act. I continue:
fourthly, to provide, on the basis of small regular payments against large and uncertain individual risks, for such hazards and disabilities as unemployment, sickness and old age.

I freely admit that unemployment could be much worse in the country than it is, but why wait until it gets worse. Why not deal with it now? It is the government's responsibility to provide either work or a subsistence income for those unemployed who are capable of working and who are willing to work. Mr. Speaker, I would like to take up again the question of bilingualism in Canada. It is a delicate subject, I admit, but so essential to good understanding between the two great races of this country that I feel I must come back to it. Even at the risk of hurting some feelings, the subject will have to be discussed time and time again until such time as true bilingualism is equally respected by the two great racial groups in this country.


I base the expediency of dealing with this matter on a statement made in this connection by His Excellency the Governor General, Right Hon. Vincent Massey, who stated in his book, "On Being Canadian", at page 20: (Text):
There are expressions of bonne entente on both sides, but one cannot build national unity simply on an exchange of compliments. The real compliment between friends is an honest expression of views in the light of mutual understanding.
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, I doubt if anybody would deny that bilingualism is the main link between the two great races which give this national unity of ours its bicultural character. It therefore follows that the vitality of national unity in this country is largely dependent upon the healthy state of this bilingualism.
May I be allowed to quote certain figures that will illustrate the present state of bilingualism and the condition of that highway to national unity. The figures I am about to quote are from the federal census of 1951, and I find them in an analysis published in the April 1954 issue of Relations, page 111 and following. According to those figures the bilingual population of Canada in 1951 was 12-3 per cent of the whole, as against 12-8 per cent in 1941.
It appears, therefore, that bilingualism is inadequate in this country, in spite of the bilingual character of our constitution. Then, too, it has shown a slight decrease in the last ten years, a fact which contradicts the too frequent statements we hear to the effect that bilingualism is gaining ground in Canada.
In addition, 60 per cent of those few bilingual people are from the province of Quebec and the great majority of bilingual people in other provinces are of French descent. Again according to the federal census of 1951, 3-8 per cent only of Canadians of English descent are bilingual.
These few figures lead to the sad conclusion that there is, properly speaking, no true bilingualism in Canada as conceived by the spirit and letter of confederation, since, barring a few exceptions, the only bilingualism practised has been purely and simply a concession on the part of the minority towards the majority. According to the same census, French Canadians, 31 per cent of whom are bilingual, supply 77-5 per cent of all the bilingual people in the country, whereas Anglo-Canadians, of whom only 3'8 per cent are bilingual, supply 14-6 per cent of all bilingualism in Canada.

The tragic conclusion to be drawn from this situation is that the only effort towards genuine good understanding has been made by French Canadians, who make up the only group to have practised a bilingualism worthy 3f mention.
Well, Mr. Speaker, instead of rejoicing over our worthier effort, we should perhaps feel sad because, when it is a one-sided practice, bilingualism becomes a neat form of assimilation. Before continuing to preach bilingualism among our compatriots, we have reached the point where we have to demand it from our English-speaking fellow citizens; otherwise, I repeat, our bilingualism will become a polite method of anglicization.
Some might bring forward the oft repeated cliche that our bilingualism has given us a practical superiority in the social development of the nation. There again, Mr. Speaker, figures deny this statement which has so often misled our French-speaking compatriots.
To convince us, let us see what bilingualism has brought us, in the very heart of Canadian life, namely in the federal civil service.
Setting aside gratuitous assertions, I have endeavoured to compile some figures which would give as accurate an idea as can be given of our representation in our federal civil service. For that purpose I took the public accounts for 1954, and went over the list of high officials in the various departments, taking those who earn more than $5,000 per year. Taking down the total number of high officials in each department, I counted every French Canadian name and established the average for each department. One may object that such a method cannot be accurate since, very likely, there are French Canadians with English names and vice versa, names which I must have missed in computing my average. I will answer immediately that argument with a reference from the 1951 federal census, which gives us the proportion of people in both ethnic groups who changed from one language to the other.
In 1951, there were in Canada 61,291 people of British origin who gave French as their mother tongue, and 342,678 people of French origin who stated that English was their mother tongue. That shows that any trend toward assimilation is more than five to one against us, which proves that the margin of error resulting from possibly mis-

Contrast that with the 25 per cent Canadian tax and you have an explanation of the major reason why a car costs so much more in Canada than in the United States. The Canadian automobile industry used to enjoy a substantial export market which has now practically disappeared owing to high production costs, of which taxation is an important element, thereby reducing employment to Canadian workmen. In 1953 the automotive distributors of Canada paid to the manufacturers the sum of $162,765,000 on the 483,821 motor vehicles

Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate it is not my intention to needlessly take up a lot of valuable time. I feel however that in the interests of the people of the Jasper-Edson constituency whom I have the honour to represent I am obligated to comment on some of the legislation forecast in the speech from the throne and also the lack of legislation to deal adequately with some of our most serious problems in my part of the country.
I should like to compliment those who have taken part in this debate thus far. The seriousness and high standard of the debate thus far is indicative of a sincere desire on the part of all members of this house to seriously and honestly appraise the proposed legislation and do something about it. I need only mention the dispatch with which the emergency legislation relating to the unemployment situation was carried out. There are many who felt that this was not the answer to this problem, but they know of the serious plight of those who depend upon the take-home pay of a husband, a father or brother. They know also of the

worry and fear and privation that always rears its head in homes where the breadwinner, through no fault of his own, is unable to provide the necessaries of life. Many of us feel that with a proper economic policy this would have been unnecessary, but nevertheless, when an emergency arose, with a minimum of political drum-beating we applied the milk of human kindness and did the only thing possible under the circumstances.
We in the opposition groups are supposed to be ever critical of government policy; we are expected to condemn the government for both their sins of commission and omission. I should like to say that I for one would like to be a little more realistic in my approach to these things. I believe in giving credit where it is due. I can see for instance some very humanitarian legislation in the Disabled Persons Act that is to take effect as of January 1 this year, and in the amendment to the Blind Persons Act, and the proposed amendments to the War Veterans Allowance Act, and others which I hope to deal with at some future date.
I was somewhat disappointed, however, in the very restricted application of the Disabled Persons Act. I sincerely hope it will not interfere with the welfare of those already enjoying more generous consideration by our Alberta provincial government. To the possible recipients of these benefits in other provinces I am sure it will be welcome news to know that nearly all of the provincial governments are setting up the necessary enabling legislation to make this assistance available at the earliest possible moment.
I am sure we are all very happy with the proposed amendment to the Blind Persons Act which allows a reduction in age to 18 years and a higher permissible income for all recipients. This is very commendable.
It is very gratifying indeed to know that at last the war veterans are going to receive more generous consideration. I would strongly urge the government to adhere to the requests of the veterans for an increase in pension to $60 per month for single men and $120 per month for married men, and to allow a permissible income of not less than $1,200 a year for single men and $2,000 a year for married men. It is not indicative of the generosity of the Canadian people to pay tribute on November 11 in such glowing terms to our glorious dead and then go home and forget about the welfare of the veterans still alive and trying to exist on a pension whose purchasing power has shrunk to 50 per cent or less of its original value. I appeal to the government to give the veterans a better deal.

I would urge the government to give serious thought at the same time to the plight of our senior citizens, and do everything possible to improve their standard of living. I have in my possession a list of comparative prices of commodities in 1927, when the old age security pension was set up, and 1955, compiled for the senior citizens association of British Columbia. This list contains 30 different items and includes such items as tea, coffee, sugar, flour, vegetables, meat and the rest of the commodities that make up the basic standard of living in the average home. In checking over the list I find that the cost of these commodities has increased by 238 per cent in the period between 1927 and 1955. Surely this alone would urge the government to give their kindest consideration to the plight of our senior citizens.
My constituency of Jasper-Edson is basically an agricultural area. This year the farmers in this area have had one of the poorest crops in their history. To start with, the rivers, I think without exception, all overflowed their banks, in some cases cutting new channels through farms and depositing on summer-fallowed fields huge deposits of gravel. When the water receded it gave the fields the appearance of a gravel pit.
This was bad enough in itself, but many of the farmers had their livestock drowned. I know of one man who lost eleven of his best cows by drowning.
Again, as if to add insult to injury, it rained almost every day all summer, either preventing the sowing of any crops or that which was seeded to mature before a very early frost came along and froze everything. As if that were not enough, we had an unusual amount of hail.
The ironical part of it all is that in many instances these same farmers have been contributing to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act since 1939 and now when misfortune overtook them they found they were out of bounds or did not qualify for one reason or another. It is not very comforting to those who have lost everything to be told that because of this technicality or that they do not qualify, and then look a little farther south or east and see their neighbour enjoying at least the minimum P.F.A.A. benefits. They feel that they have been paying money into P.F.A.A. since 1939 under false pretences. It may be that they do not understand the mechanics of P.F.A.A., whatever they might be. I say that these people deserve a better deal and I urge the government to do everything possible at the earliest possible moment to help these fine people.
We have heard of the merits of NATO and the desirability of international co-operation in world affairs, and we recognize this as
The Address-Mr. Villeneuve desirable; but I would remind the members of this house that charity begins at home, and until we have learned how to manage our own affairs and look after our own people we are not setting a very good example to those we desire to help.

Mr. Speaker, I find that in my constituency unemployment does not cause as much concern now as it did last year. However we have seasonal unemployment and it is a problem which requires our attention as well as all our ingenuity if we want to solve it.
The government brought in amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act which will bring some relief to those people out of work, especially this winter. May I however be allowed to draw attention to some connection between unemployment and public works. The unemployment insurance benefits paid to those who are entitled to them must not constitute an encouragement to idleness. It is said that the devil finds work for idle hands to do and that is why I think that we should implement some public works project which would bear some relation to the payment of benefits. We might see to it that these people are paid the benefits to which they are entitled and ask the Department of Public Works to make up the rest of their salary. Our people like to work. In all our constituencies there are lots of things to be done and it is a pity that those people who would like to work should be unemployed.
Another point worth mentioning, I think, is that of assistance to small industries. We could certainly improve their position by amending the Industrial Development Bank Act. This legislation is somewhat too rigid for my liking. It should not only help in the expansion of industries operating at present, but it should more particularly assist in the establishment of small new industries with a view to diversifying the Canadian economy. In fact, if, in every community of any size at all, there were one or two small plants I feel sure that that would improve the labour and agricultural situation with consequent benefits to our working classes as a whole.
The 1954 housing act has had excellent results so far. I must point out though that these advantages have not been visible in my own constituency since the banks have not seen fit to give it all the desired attention. I would, however, like to say a word about one class of people who are in an unfortunate position as far as housing is concerned. I am thinking of our large families. I think it may safely be said that no group of people in this country is as badly housed as our large families. Yet, as has often been pointed out,


are they not the best human asset a country can have? In what way, then, could we bring special attention to their plight in the matter of housing? I know, of course, that it is much easier to advocate ideas than to solve problems. But I think that it would be a good thing, especially in semi-urban constituencies to come back to the general idea of the joint loan, with one-half being advanced by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and the other by a recognized lending institution.
Central Mortgage and Housing would lend at an interest rate equal to that of government bonds, whereas the approved lending institution could lend at prevailing rates. Thus, in due course, the interest rate would probably fall to 4J or 4} per cent. Then, by continuing the mortgage insurance and promoting low cost housing, we could probably house a high proportion of the large families of this country who are particularly in need of shelter. This could be done only if benefits of the act were made available to all, everywhere in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, ten years ago, a Liberal government-and I think it can be said Liberal governments were always those to alleviate suffering in this country through social security measures-instituted family allowances. Since then, this same government, having remained in power, have improved matters by enacting other measures equally appreciated by the people of this country.
I can say that in my particular constituency families are generally large and greatly appreciate family allowances. In view of the high cost of living, they are under the obligation of asking that these allowances be increased, without further affecting the pocket book of the Canadian taxpayer. As large families are an asset to the country, I ask the government to be more generous to the heads of these families in granting them increased allowances and to give them very special consideration.
I wish the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) were in his seat at this time. However, I know that he will take notice of the particular request I want to make on behalf of my constituents.
In fact, for some years, numerous Canadians have been asking, in the name of national unity and to further adorn the crown of national unity through understanding and justice, that cheques issued throughout the country be bilingual. We acknowledge that much has been done up till now, because all cheques issued in the province of Quebec are bilingual. That is, so to speak, only a beginning. I should now like to see the government continue its work and the Minister

of Finance give favourable consideration to this request, which I believe to be quite fair and reasonable, namely, bilingual cheques throughout the country.
To my knowledge, bilingual stamps and currency have caused no social or racial disturbances likely to injure national unity. I should rather say that these measures have contributed to the consolidation of national unity. I am convinced that the hon. Minister of Finance will give serious consideration to our request and make a favourable decision. Besides, I have read a letter he wrote to an organization fighting for this cause and it is my belief that we shall soon hear good news about bilingual cheques.
I have a further request to make, regarding the simultaneous translation of the debates of this house. I think it would be an improvement. I can hardly lay claim to perfect bilingualism. On the contrary, I have much to do before I reach that point. However, I am trying real hard to get there and I am glad to realize that many English-speaking members are doing the same. They deserve congratulations and encouragement, for the sake of national unity.
The more bilingual Canadians there are in this country, the easier it will be for the two racial groups to understand each other better and to be in greater sympathy. They will be glad to live together in the same country, enjoying the same freedom and mutual understanding.
I understand that in such countries as Belgium and Switzerland, where they have two or three official languages, there is simultaneous translation of debates, as at United Nations headquarters. To my mind, this system would help give justice to all.
Yesterday, I heard the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Cannon) refer to a statement reported to have been made in Vancouver by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch). I am of the opinion that if a system of simultaneous interpretation were established in this house, the hon. member for Vancouver East would not have complained of the fact that we speak French here and that he has to wait 24 hours to get the translation of a speech made in French. With simultaneous translation, we could all convey our ideas to one another, our speeches would be understood immediately. Moreover, we could all give our full measure here since, if I am not mistaken, out of 265 members of the house only about 15 are perfectly bilingual. Simultaneous interpretations would certainly increase, not reduce, our incentive to learn both languages. Such a system would
The Address-Mr. Villeneuve help us also to grasp the meaning of everything which takes place here, since it is especially hard in this corner to catch certain statements and certain speeches, a condition which bars us from maximum efficiency.
We must also consider the visitors who understand only one language. They would be able to listen to the translation of the speech being made. They would get more satisfaction and be more interested in the proceedings, as would too the members themselves.
May I be permitted now, Mr. Speaker, to come to the main topic of my speech, agriculture.
In the constituency of Roberval, which it is my privilege to represent in this house, 60 to 65 per cent of the population devote their time to agriculture. This agricultural activity, I believe, constitutes the very backbone of the riding from the economic point of view.
Numerous individuals and organizations from my constituency have asked me to request that the right hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and the government maintain at 58 cents a pound for two more years the support price for butter.
That request is exceedingly important for all the farmers in my constituency as well as for all the farmers of Quebec. In this regard I would like to quote from a speech made by the dairy industry commissioner for the province of Quebec:
Too little thought, perhaps, is given to the importance of the dairy industry of the province of Quebec with its capitalization reaching one and a quarter billion dollars, including $225 million for herds, aggregating about a million head of cattle, which produced, last year, five and a half billion pounds of milk, the gross worth of which on the farm was $168,569,000, or $11 million more than in 1952 and $18 million more than three years ago.
In 1952, 33 per cent of the total agricultural income of the province of Quebec came from the dairy industry. In 1953, that proportion had reached nearly 40 per cent. It should be noted that Quebec is the province most dependent on its dairy industry for its general agricultural prosperity. Indeed, except for Nova Scotia and British Columbia, the percentage of farm income derived from the production of milk in all other provinces including Ontario, is under 20 per cent.
One cannot stress too strongly the fact that half a million people derive their living directly from the dairy industry; to that number must be added those who depend on it indirectly, such as people employed in the processing, transportation and distribution of dairy products, the manufacture of machinery and accessories and those who provide essential services to the dairy industry. It all adds up to the fact that one-third of the people of Quebec depend on the prosperity of the dairy industry. It is therefore the source of an enormous purchasing power for one and a quarter million consumers of the province and it has a major influence on our economy as a whole.
The market value of dairy products, once they have been processed and have reached the market.

The Address-Mr. Villeneuve jumped from $193 million in 1951 to $207 million in 1952 and $222 million last year, an increase of more than $25 million in three years. It should be pointed out that as far as the gross value of production is concerned, the dairy industry ranks second in the province of Quebec, after the pulp and paper industry. It contributes nearly 40 per cent of the total dairy production of Canada. It produces:
34% of the butter manufactured in Canada,
21% of the Cheddar cheese made in Canada,
27% of the other kinds of cheese,
33% of the concentrated products made in Canada,
20% of the ice cream made in Canada,
32% of the whole milk sold in Canada.
I have here other statistics which are no less staggering on the importance of the problem for Quebec farmers. In 1953, 302,606,000 pounds of creamery butter were produced in Canada, of which 112,179,000 pounds came from Quebec.
Now, as for the effect of the support price of butter on the Quebec farmer's income, I must say that the farmer received 75 per cent of the retail price of butter. The farmer very seldom gets such a large share of the retail price of a consumer product. That is why the support price on butter has been more or less a lifesaver for the farmers. And it is to enable our farmers to maintain a decent standard of living and improve their position, especially as far as Quebec farmers are concerned, that I am asking the right hon. Minister of Agriculture and the government to maintain the support price on butter at 58 cents a pound for two more years.
Besides, from the Canadian standpoint, it is said that one out of six Canadians, or 17 per cent of our people, depends directly or indirectly on the dairy industry for his living. I believe that figure clearly shows the importance of the dairy industry for us.
Mr. Speaker, as I have only one more subject to discuss, may I ask this house, if it is possible, to allow me an extra five minutes after the ten o'clock bell.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are told, today, that more and more farmers are leaving the land to settle in cities. If we have to deplore an ever-increasing unemployment, seasonal unemployment, in particular, it is


because our farmers are going to the cities where they add to the number of labourers who, unfortunately, have to rely on temporary jobs for their living.
It is our duty to help keep the farmers on the land, and in so doing, we help maintain the stability of the Canadian economy, because agriculture has always been and will always be the soundest basis of society, and that is needed in this country probably more than elsewhere.
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a word or two on the subject of the building of the Chibougamau-St. Felicien railway. Last summer, I made numerous representations together with my colleague, the hon. member for Lake St. John (Mr. Gauthier), in order to bring the matter to a head. Guarantees were put up by the lumber companies, and we have not yet given up hope that the Canadian National will accept these guarantees. I plan to deal with that subject again, when this house discusses the motion introduced by the hon. member for Lake St. John. However, I think I always did my best to bring about the implementation of that project which, in my opinion, is of capital importance for the future of the economy, not only of my constituency, but also of my whole district. It has always seemed strange to me to note that those who never work for the cause are always the first to take the credit. They give us the impression they are trying to keep alive the tradition of the fly on the wheel.
Incidentally, I would like to ask the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer), whose absence is so often noticed in this house, to kindly read again what was said last year in this house and at the railway committee, in order to find out what the hon. member for Lake St. John and myself have done, within our party and outside, to have that project carried out one way or another.
I would like to tell him again, in conclusion, that I am confident the Chibougamau-St. Felicien railway will soon be built; I will continue to rely on the spirit of understanding of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler), of all the members of the cabinet, and of the Canadian National authorities for the construction in the near future of the St. Felicien-Chibougamau section of the Chibougamau railway. No doubt it will be built in my constituency, and I undertake to promote this project to which we could never give too much importance.
Mr. Speaker, I shouldn't like to overtax your patience, and I thank you for the forbearance you have shown me.
